title: The cave and the breath
hook: the Lord set the soul in the cave of the body and played the breath like music (Anand)

segments.voice: Yesterday, O my ears, and your line, ears, hear truth. Did you choose what your ears would hear for a while? Body, eyes, ears: today the Anand looks at the whole body again, from inside. Day three hundred ninety-eight.

Sit near the front of almost any gurdwara during kirtan and watch the ragi's left hand. While the right hand plays the keys of the harmonium, the left hand works the bellows at the back, folding and unfolding, steady, the whole time. Without that push of air, the keys are just wood. With it, the hall fills with sound. Guru Amar Das never saw a harmonium; it came to India centuries later. But he saw the same idea, inside every person. Today: the cave and the breath.
screen: `THE RAGI'S LEFT HAND ON THE BELLOWS.` → `NO AIR, NO MUSIC.` → `THE SAME IDEA, INSIDE A PERSON.`

segments.voice: The pauri opens, in paraphrase: the beloved Lord placed the soul inside the cave, and played the instrument of the breath. The cave, gufaa, is the body: dark, enclosed, hollow, like the caves where people in India have long gone to meditate. The instrument, vaajaa, is played by pavan, air, breath. So every breath is the Lord playing music in a cave. Then the pauri gets more specific. In that body, it says, nine doors were made plain to see, and the tenth was kept hidden. Commentators usually take the nine doors as the body's openings: the eyes, the ears, the nostrils, the mouth and the two below. The tenth door, dasvaa duaar, is hidden. Sikh teachers describe it in different ways, but most understand it as an inner opening, not a physical one, the place where a person comes to know the One. And the pauri says how it's found: through the Guru's door, with loving faith, some are shown the tenth door. There, it says, are many forms, the Name, the nine treasures, and no one can find the end of them. It closes by repeating its first line: the Lord placed the soul in the cave and played the breath. Notice the order of this week's pauris. The body was asked what it had done, told where its light came from, then the eyes and ears were given their work. Now, underneath all of it, the breath: the music nobody has to remember to play. Breath is music.
screen: `GUFAA: THE BODY AS A CAVE.` · `PAVAN: BREATH PLAYS THE INSTRUMENT.` · `NINE DOORS PLAIN, THE TENTH HIDDEN.` · `THE GURU'S DOOR SHOWS THE TENTH.` · then, large: `BREATH IS MUSIC.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: breathe and hear it. Sit still, and let the room go quiet around you. Breathe in through the nose, a little slower than usual, and listen to the sound it makes. Breathe out and listen to that sound too. In, out, like the ragi's hand on the bellows. Don't try to make it beautiful. It already is music, the pauri says. Just keep hearing it. If you pray, you can let Waheguru ride along on one breath. The bell holds the time.
The cave and the breath. In the Anand, the Lord places the soul in the cave of the body and plays the breath like an instrument; nine doors are open, and the tenth is hidden.
screen: `THE CAVE AND THE BREATH — today's word`.

segments.voice: Your line: breath is music. Today, at one moment of hurry, stop and hear three breaths go in and out, like bellows. Day three hundred ninety-eight.

howItsDone: This pauri is part of the full Anand Sahib that many Sikhs recite each morning; in the gurdwara, kirtan is commonly sung to the harmonium and tabla, and many Sikhs pair simran, remembering the Name, with the breath.

original.note: Gurmukhi: gufaa, cave; the Anand's picture of the body, where the soul is placed and the breath is played.

trapdoor: what you thought: the cave and the breath is about meditating in a cave.
what it means: the body is the cave, the soul is placed in it, and every breath is the Lord playing music.
what a scholar hears: the nine doors and the hidden tenth, dasam duaar, recur across the Guru Granth Sahib; commentators generally read the tenth as an inner opening of realization, not a bodily one.

sources.ref: Ramkali M3, Anand, the cave pauri (har jeeo gufaa andar rakh kai vaajaa pavan vajaaiaa), Ang 922

notes: The cave pauri paraphrased: soul placed in the cave, breath played as an instrument; nine doors revealed, the tenth hidden; through the Guru's door with loving faith some are shown the tenth door; many forms, the Name, the nine treasures, no end found. Commonly numbered pauri 38. Confirm numbering, Ang and glosses.

The nine doors as the bodily openings and the tenth door as an inner opening: standard commentary, but interpretations of dasam duaar vary (some yogic readings place it at the crown of the head). Phrased as 'most understand'; confirm.
'Guru Amar Das never saw a harmonium; it came to India centuries later': the hand harmonium reached India in the nineteenth century. Confirm.
